en: He who, though one, is divided threefold for the sake of the self-delight in creation, maintenance, and dissolution— by means of the powers (śaktis) presided over by the lotus-born Brahmā, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, and the three-eyed Śiva, who are radiant with the rays of the fire, moon, and sun, and born from the Udgītha, which is rich in the three qualities (traiguṇya).
Salutations to that Śiva, the eternal consciousness, the all-pervading lord, for the king’s accomplishment of his goals.

(1cd) His form, adorned by the crescent of the new moon, is recognized as the supreme seed of the Triple Veda; it brings about the emergence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and is divided threefold by its constituent parts. (2ab)

The sages declare that the imperishable (akṣara), which is to be attained through yoga, is directly [the goal]; may there be salutation for the sake of perfect accomplishment unto that Blessed One, Śiva, whose self is the Praṇava.
She who was formerly the sole one, whose gait was like the graceful movement of a swan, who was beloved, and whose mind was fixed on the Supreme (unmanā), being virtuous— [may she grant you grace].

May that supreme Gaurī protect you— she who, having pierced her own body to ascend to the sky for the sake of her beloved, has attained youth once more; she who bears a lotus born from Lake Mānasa, made to blossom by the radiance of her own luster, and who brings about the arising of union with Śiva.

May that Blessed One, the cause of all causes, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon, be victorious— he who, by means of his eight own bodies consisting of the sacrificer, the sacrificial fire, light, wind, ether, earth, water, and the moon, pervades these worlds, thereby manifesting his unimpeded causal power in a manner that is beyond words.
Bow down to Nārāyaṇa, who, spreading his sovereign power,
traversed the three worlds in a mere three steps,
as if even now desiring to attain a fourth state.
Under the guise of sleep, he enters meditative absorption within the ocean—
he who, born from the lotus, triumphs as he utters with his four faces a sound equal to the roar of the clouds of the syllable *oṃ*;
he who, for the sake of filling the three worlds at their arising, seems to lead his own primordial seed, sown in the field, to a state of swelling.
Victorious is the Mandākinī, whose streams issue from the orb of the gentle-rayed moon, held upon the head of Dhūrjaṭi;
she flows forth pre-eminently as if to demonstrate the continuity of his love for her who is joined with half the body of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
From the ocean [of fame] there arose one whose feet were honored by the garlands of crest-jewels of sovereigns.
The king named Bālāditya— also known as the full moon that causes the lotuses of his enemies' clans to wither,

the ornament upon the vault of the sky that is the Soma-Kauṇḍinya lineage, and a ruler of vast renown— carried the fortune of sovereignty, which filled the blameless city illuminated by his staff-like arms.
Bestowing upon his utterly haughty enemies in battle the rite of initiation into widowhood for their wives,
he binds with his virtues a garland of excellent fame, white as the rays of the moon,
in the city of the gateway to heaven— a city that rivals and surpasses the city of Indra. (9ab)
Sārva installed the Śārva Liṅga, endowed with great power and accompanied by the prescribed rites.
His sister’s daughter, a virtuous woman who brought about the prosperity of the succession of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, bore the auspicious name Sarasvatī and was renowned as the purifier of the world.
He went to his beloved Viśvarūpa, the best of the twice-born and a most profound vessel for the words of various scriptures, just as the ocean goes to the king of rivers;
he was the very essence of the lineage of his own family, beginning with Soma, which had now passed away despite its great splendor.

Born from the milk-ocean of that lineage, she was as noble as the Pārijāta tree of her blossoming fame; accompanied by the foremost of gods, beginning with Rudra, Upendra, and Indra, for the sake of the Nandana grove,
that pure maiden, who brings benefit to the world, obtained birth like a second Lakṣmī.
She who is called Mahendradevī even by name, the sovereign lady who is the daughter of a mountain king, her praises being sung repeatedly by celestial nymphs;
[and] the son of the lord of the earth, born from the lineage of the Sun, the prince of the lord of Bhavapura. 12ab
Having attained her, King Mahendravarman exercised lordship over the entire earth;

with his darkness of vice destroyed, he surpassed the mild-rayed moon in its splendor, while through that husband who had manifested such ascetic power, he established a continuous succession of lotuses among his subjects.
From that queen Aditi, as the sun was produced by Kaśyapa,
there arose the illustrious King Rājendravarman, a treasury of splendors.
He was like the full moon from the ocean of milk, or like the fire from the sun-gem.
He who was born of a pure lineage, utterly purified and honored by all kings,
appeared [like the sun]. The manifestation of splendor, the destruction of darkness, the clarity of the quarters, and the blossoming of the arts—
whatever function belongs to the hot-rayed sun and the cool-rayed moon, he performed it all at his rising.
The *santānaka* tree, though already delightful and pleasant due to its abundant and continuous blossoming,
reached the pinnacle of loveliness by attaining in great measure that which yields magnificent fruit.
Growing day by day with an ever-increasing and intensely charming splendor, his body became preeminently captivating.
He who, bringing about the rise of all sides, indeed eclipsed the splendor of the moon;
he who, even in childhood, was so swiftly filled with arts and daily radiant with the quality of eloquence,
that he cast far beneath him even the moon’s possession of digits, which is accompanied by dullness.
Having cast aside the occasion for faults, she shines forth, illuminating the meaning as it pervades the world;
such is the splendor of that speaker who, like the dawn, possesses a faultless face through his learning.
Having attained the unfailing power consisting of knowledge, bestowed by Maheśvara and brought forth by the wise, [he speaks].
In his youth, he who had conquered the host of his enemies illuminated the splendor of Mahendra;
he, born of a noble lineage, renowned for his abundance of virtues, preeminent in prowess, and highly esteemed,
bent that great bow and lofty Kṣatriya clan alike through his training.

Having immediately adopted that which was taught by the learned, he made that field supreme—a field that ripens even without being ploughed—by irrigating it with the water of faith; and there he sowed the preeminent seeds of both the scripture and the weapon, which sprouted and grew tall. He who, through his mastery, always maintained a particular excellence of brilliance, setting aside all other qualities from every side.
Free from sloth, he daily took up [his duties] for the welfare of the world, as the sun draws up the juices.
23cd Like the wealth of spring to a garden, like the full-moon night to the moon, the splendor of his fresh youth blossomed forth, enhancing his extraordinary beauty. 24ab–24cd
Even though the complete characteristics of a great man were already established by nature in him,
he revealed his state as Maheśvara through some [divine power], like the teachings of the Asaṅkhya;
for that abundant beauty of his, which had increased from childhood and was unattainable by any other, [was manifest].
Surely the Creator fashioned her limbs, coloring them with the abundant splendor of youth;
for even though her fresh youth was fully manifest, the god of love, constantly suppressed by her,
did not approach her out of pride, as if born of shame at the sight of such beauty.
Seeing his bodily loveliness, which was unmatched by any other, Rati closed her eyes out of love;
I believe she did not even perceive her own husband as he was consumed by the flames from the eye of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Possessing great power through the drawing of his bow, that heroic youth attained the fortune of a crown prince.
He who, like Rāma, married the virtuous Sītā, born not from a womb but brought forth by the Creator;
from that time on, his prosperity increased, as if by the consecration of the water of immortality flowing from the golden jars [of the sun] from the solar orb, or like the splendor of the moon.
The fire of his splendor grew intense through the waters of his lineage, which were never barren of mantras;
and as if in rivalry with that, the fire of grief among his enemies also blazed up simultaneously with the falling tears of their eyes.
Adorned with innate virtues such as learning and the like, and with his own heart-pleasing limbs that were naturally beautiful, he was truly embellished.
By means of that accumulation of non-rustic ornaments, he adopted the auspicious adornment. He, who had just completed his great consecration and was wearing fresh jewel-ornaments,
bore the splendor of the ocean— which had its waters drunk up by the jar-born [Agni] and whose heaps of jewels had emerged— just as it does when its waters are newly drained.
Though his form was as if seized by fear of the planets that had ascended to high positions— both great and small—
he was himself placed upon the lion-throne, lofty as a mountain of gold, even though he desired it not.
I believe that no other object of comparison could possibly exist that is so irreproachable as the splendor of his limbs.
Even a reflection that has been transferred to the surface of a mirror is rendered unworthy by the nature of its support;

yet, when he was consecrated, the earth—with its beautiful ocean-girdle became wet by the falling water—and it raised up his fame, white as a shimmering crescent moon, like a single royal parasol held aloft. (35–36)
He proclaimed the fruit of all perfections characterized by their own specific marks as his immediate maturation,
for which the blessings uttered by the assembly of brahmins became like mere repetitions of what was already established.
Like swarms of bees around a *pārijāta* tree, or like the intellects of sages toward self-yoga, [they were drawn to him].
Abandoning all other activities for the worlds, his eyes fell upon him alone.
The flickering splendor of the kings’ glories, naturally transient like lightning flashing here and there,
remained so until the beautiful autumn appeared, cloudless and providing the perfect occasion for his expedition.
He whose splendor was radiant from the purification-rite of fierce weapons, who blazed with initiation into the great maṇḍala,
and who had secured his own self-protection through the mantras of the limbs of knowledge, achieved success of noble magnificence.
When he set out for world conquest, he deployed an army of banners with fluttering flags.
First the Fortune of his enemies' kings trembled, and afterwards the earth, heavy with the burden of his army;

for when his enemies from afar heard the sound of his trumpets— resembling the roar of Saumitri as he advanced after vanquishing Meghanāda— they were struck with fear, as if they were the equals of the Ten-faced one himself.
The mass of dust raised by his army as he marched, like a column of smoke from the fire of his majesty,
touched even the eyes of the wives of his enemies and caused them to shed tears. Having first covered the earth, it then proceeded to fill the streams with turbidity through its own dust.
His vehicle surged forward, like an army of hosts risen in fury;
in some places it was strewn with shattered mountains and pursued by enemy forces,
while in other places, as he advanced, his path became as vast as the course of the celestial river.
He who, by means of his forces, rendered every evil deed of the people powerless and destroyed their manifest activity by forcibly suppressing all obstacles throughout the enemy's city with darkness;
he, like Garuḍa, having spread his two wings and uttered a roar, entered that place with speed.
The host of two elephants, their prowess and strength destroyed, stood there bewildered as to where they should go.
(47) Wherever he put on his armor with boldness, like the sun in its brilliance... and wherever he was, he dissolved into the earth like a lotus-pond scorched by heat. (48)
In that battle, which appeared like the clear autumn season,
the light kings became as futile as clouds scattered here and there by the wind as they hid themselves;
for he, wielding a bow resembling Indra’s rainbow, roared and rained down a shower of arrows.
He swiftly released arrows at the mountain-like lord of monkeys, just as Bālāhaka pours down rain upon a great mountain. Having encountered the enemy host,
which was like a flock of moths approaching a fire, the group of foes felt as if they had attained joy, though they were truly deluded.
The blazing fire of splendor, produced from the friction-sticks of his staff-like arms, which had entered into his calamity;
by whose speed he was sent forth, having grown in the sky, consuming the trees, the rivers, and the mountains of the earth.
Having reached his own seat, having cast down his enemies, and having blocked the path of the winds as well as the course of his mind,
the rain of arrows remained fixed upon him as he practiced, like a yogic power that has mastered even the supersensory realm.
His heads, splendors, and lofty riches were all gathered together.
In battle, he withdrew [his arrows] together with his shafts. 54.
The feathered arrows, released from his bow, fell upon the heads of his enemies, charming with their whizzing sound;
yet they were followed by the fragrance of Mandāra flowers released from the creeper-like hands of the celestial beauties. 55.
He who,

though obstructed by the lords of his enemies in battle upon a mountain-like foe, shone forth with the stream of blood flowing from the wounds of weapons, having severed the heads of the multitude of kings as if they were mere creepers. 56.
Just as the sun, when completely obscured by the shadow of a cloud, abandons its own radiance while wearing a thin veil;
so too [the hero],
whose fame was spread abroad by his valor, led away the evil-hearted Daśānana from the midst of the battle-hosts.
Neither did the wielder of the discus desire to take up his wheel in battle, nor was the son of Indra victorious even with his thunderbolt;
for he who, though possessed of power and having conquered the host of his enemies, had received the most unbearable weapon of Maheśvara,
remained free from fear after warding off the enemy army.
Yet his heart, though pierced by the arrows of those wanton women, remained itself undisturbed.
For he did not lose his composure even while being churned by the enemy's weapons in battle, owing to his profound gravity;
for a lake may indeed become turbid from the contact with elephants, but the ocean never does.
He trembled in every direction, his chest heaving;
like a flash of lightning, the tongue of that serpent-like arm flickered straight yet seemed crooked as it quivered.
He who, when his enemy was struck down by a further blow, suffered greatly the reproach of being "armless";
he who, for the sake of bringing down celestial damsels, created as it were a perfect staircase;
and he who, having divided his own side's protection from the means of refutation and proof, launched an attack upon the enemy's vulnerability.

Being skillful, he rendered his opponent speechless, depriving him of his subsequent course of action; [he did so] by making the enemy's own passion result in his own defeat. He, the successful one, imitated in battle the conduct of Fate, who acts perversely toward that which is ordained.
Though entreated by her friend to face him, and though the enemy host desired boldness,
it turned its back from afar upon him who was like a newly-wed bride seeing her husband at the arrival of the wedding fire—
[he] who was joined in that great battle with the Goddess of Victory.
"Indeed, it has been rightly said by those who know the principles of logic that the perfection of valor is not without purpose:

even the host of his enemies, dwelling in the forest clad in deer-skins, stands like a pillar—powerless, their bodies discolored by contact with the fortress, their eyes restless as they peer out from the openings of caves. (68cd–69)
...the desire of the bridegroom was rendered futile;
for although the earth was vast, it was not sufficient for his ambition to conquer it, nor was it enough for his generosity, as there were always suppliants.
70ab–cd The ocean, with its swaying and burgeoning clusters of bright coral, had its serpents submerged beneath the treading of Hari. 71ab
Because of its internal forests and inaccessibility, it was like the ocean; even the territory of his enemies abandoned their prosperity.

(71cd) ... Endowed with effort for the accomplishment of his goals, he seized the four quarters—the paths of which were unknown—to increase the three constituents, just as one acquires branches of knowledge in childhood. (72ab–72cd)
His fame, having secured space through its sovereignty in the world, untouched by other great qualities, enjoys the connection with the quality of sound, like the stainless sky. [73] ...
[she whose body was] emaciated by wasting, [healed] previously by the investigation of the conduct and teachings of Suśruta. [74]
He who was exceedingly skillful in destroying every fault nourished the earth with its six flavors;
that very splendor which had previously conquered other splendors, and that same great circle of dominion,
blazed intensely once he had attained great sovereignty, like the sun at midday.
When that one of intense splendor ascended the lion-throne, which resembled a mountain with a roaring lion,
not only did the stars lose their luster, but the jeweled crowns of rival kings fell as well.
When his great white parasol, possessing the beauty of the moon, was raised aloft, [it eclipsed all else].
Having abandoned the entire earth, the heat [of his splendor] assailed the minds of his enemies;
for surely, all the worlds, long impelled by the desire to behold his form,
repeatedly sought through countless sacrifices the state of being unblinking [gods], in order to achieve their own long-cherished wish.
Desiring to see his innate prosperity reflected among his friends, he gradually transferred it to them—

just as one who has finished using his ornaments might transfer his own reflection from a polished gem-mirror to other mirrors— even while he himself remained adorned. His policy, owing to its extreme brilliance, was exceedingly straightforward, unlike that of others.

Except for the sun and the moon, what other planet possesses a retrograde or otherwise contrary motion? (80cd) He, by means of the four expedients beginning with conciliation—rooted in wise counsel—and through various applications, as well as by the Vedas and those skillful means that block the path to ruin, achieved complete success. (81)
Though he is always recognized as the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), he displays various great deeds;

through the application of the six political measures (*ṣāḍguṇya*), he proclaimed the three qualities (*triguṇa*) of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), which is incomparable, even without the use of speech.
Generally, even a crooked fate (*vidhi*) exerts its power over that which is to be ordained through the specific strengths of counsel, majesty, and prowess.
As if out of fear,

the calamities of his realm— being far surpassed by the floods of his virtues which were like friends through their association with the three goals of life— fled to the side of his enemies as if in anger. (83cd–84)
He who, having immediately pierced through his own fault, rose up and by means of reason subdued other wrongdoers—
he, like the maker of night, destroys even the darkness yet disregards his own entire stain.
For when a king rules well and is free from vice, no fear of calamity arises among his subjects.
Even Ajātaśatru’s princess suffered great distress in the past because of Duḥśāsana.

(86cd) Having obtained that king as a worthy vessel, the fortunes of power—though difficult to restrain, waiting for a lapse, and possessing a nature that is easily agitated by those who have broken their own luster—became as firmly established as water in a well-crafted receptacle. (87)

Having subdued the host of predatory enemies on their path by means of his power, which moved like a lioness about him, he nurtured the earth— whose subjects were uplifted through his union with her— and having obtained Lakṣmī as his queen, he attained sovereignty. Thus, the assembly of wise men ranked Kārtavīrya at the head of all great kings, despite his thousand faults.

When even the fame of Arjuna—who had acquired a wealth of valor and whose glory was sung throughout both heaven and earth—was not born as a fit object of comparison for his fame, which was pleasing to the ears and capable of providing such pleasure to the listener that nothing else could match it, then what further need is there to speak of him who is truly never deficient in any virtue? (89cd–90ab) [Note: The numbering and phrasing follow the provided source text.]

When his noble fame had first thundered, pervading the quarters and the sky like a rain-cloud, the land of Vidarbha did not merely present him with jewels as a tribute, but swiftly offered elephants and other such gifts. He, who—
by means of the columns of smoke arising from hundreds of thousands of sacrifices, which shrouded the directions and eclipsed the rays of the sun— [rendered the world dark].
He simultaneously brought both heaven and the fame of Indra to a state of defilement.
The inference of fire from the sight of smoke is said to be non-deviant;
however, the inference of rain from the gods based on the sight of sacrificial smoke is indeed new.

To him who, though empty, became filled according to his desire upon reaching those who approached him of their own accord— like the ocean which, even without being asked, is full with waters that are perfect riches— and who, like a rain-cloud,
rained down for the multitude of supplicants; who, though captivating to the eye and mind, displayed the beauty of the tips of his hands, moist with the essence of true flavor.
The lunar orb of him who conducts himself with auspicious conduct is worthy of comparison to a dance, yet it is not blemished by a deer;

even another king, though merely relying on its shadow, is capable of conquering arrogant enemies—how much more so he himself? Let the sun, whose great splendor has been transferred [to the moon], be set aside for now; does the moon not dispel the thick darkness?
She displayed other ornaments that possessed great splendor, such as a jeweled mirror;

for the beauty of her own nails served as a mirror for the kings, who wore them as their ear-ornaments according to their command. Even another person, though equal to someone in some quality, does not attain the same greatness as she did.
For by the mere vow of dancing, the blue-throated peacock attains lordship;

(98cd) She whose course is ever-constant, who bestows affection, and who maintains vast sovereignty while bearing great radiance—she supports the arrangement of the worlds within her, just as fame composed of the great elements sustains the world. (99ab–99cd)
He was created by the Creator with deliberate intent as the sole abode, even more preeminent than those qualities such as generosity, heroism, physical grace, profundity, sweetness, and compassion;
he whose valor on earth was already renowned as Kārtavīrya, yet whose prowess was previously surpassed by the strength of his two arms.
If one were to look upon a person who, for the sake of his own sustenance, considers himself to have thousands of hands, I think that person would be like one who,
having conquered enemies from afar through his majesty, finds actual combat utterly impossible— just as a scent-elephant, fierce with rut, has terrified other elephants by its very odor.
Having abandoned attachment to other deities, those who possess supreme faith and devotion toward Him—
like Gaṅgā and Bhavānī approaching Śrīkaṇṭha, the God of gods, with longing—
the Creator, as it were, displays the very pinnacle of all beauty.

"He whom the Creator fashioned as the single pillar of gold for the world; he who, being exceedingly handsome, was brought to lordship by the Ordainer as if to say, 'In this manner, my desire has been fulfilled, though it was indeed burnt by the wielder of the Pināka.'"
People considered him clever in all four branches of knowledge;
he was rich in the sixty-four arts, like the four-faced Lord Prajāpati.
Having placed Lakṣmī upon his chest, he cast his fame across the ocean.
He who, though young, took delight with Vṛddhā alone out of devotion to sacred knowledge;
Dilīpa, who formerly protected the cow of Vasiṣṭha out of a desire for progeny;
and he who, having obtained the earth through his own prowess, [gave it] to the descendant of Bhṛgu along with his offspring.
In that ocean of milk which is his fame— overflowing with the deluge that submerges the worlds—
the earth, out of fear, has surely taken refuge in the moon under the guise of its reflection.
He who, though filled with a thousand coils, bears even the burden of the earth.
Though endowed with infinite virtues, he is a great remover of the distress of the humble; by him,
who covered the earth adorned with the expanse of the ocean-girdle under a single great umbrella,
Mount Meru was rendered insignificant.
Due to contact with the thorns of strife and because of stumbling through the loss of his footing,
Dharma— who had descended [into the world]— remained well-established by taking refuge in him.
In battle, the smoke-bannered fire of his majesty was fanned by the wind of his prowess.
Though free from smoke, it increased the streams of tears of the wives of his two enemies.
The Goddess of Fortune, possessing a splendor like a flash of lightning, remained steadfastly attached to Yama;
yet fame, though bound by its connection to virtues, was carried away to every quarter by someone.
Whose arm was like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) with its sword-blade as a red sprout, planted in the Śrīnandana grove of battle, scattered the flowers of his fame throughout the quarters;
[he whose] chariot, struck by the blows from the tusks of proud lordly elephants, [proceeded]. 115–116ab.
In his wrath, he covered the great beings with thick dust as if with the earth itself.
Having offered the lotus-faces of his enemies into the fire of his sword— kindled by fuel and strengthened by the power of mantras— he brought forth imperial sovereignty.
By him, who possesses infinite power, the enemy— though firm, of unassailable spirit, and lofty—
was uprooted like a mountain born of a noble lineage during the churning of the ocean;
and the fortune of his foes, as if parched with thirst, was utterly consumed by the fire of his splendor.
Having received whose stream born of the lotus, he did not cast it down for even a moment;
and whose dust from the lotus-feet, as if imitating his own conduct,
bestowed glory by setting foot upon the lofty peaks of the best of mountains.
He who, with a belly that bore offspring while his eyes were closed in sleep,
is Hari, the Lord of the heart, whose prowess is clearly manifest through perfect awakening;
he who, having conquered the haughty lord of enemies in battle, showed favor to that dynasty.
For what indeed is a lordly elephant to a king of beasts when it is distracted by the intoxication of bees?
Having bound his beloved sword with arrows endowed with virtues—
straight shafts— he conquered his enemies and enjoyed wealth as if through excellent qualities.
The poison was drunk by the blue-throated one as an ornament for his neck;
yet it was he who, for the sake of pleasing the gods, vomited forth the nectar of speech.
By whose thick, ascending sacrificial smoke, which obstructed the vision of all, [the world was filled].
Even now, the sun is surely made to wander through the quarters by his own steeds, who have lost their way;
he who, having kindled the fire of his majesty with the fuel-sticks of his enemies in the sacrifice of battle,
bestowed upon the twice-born birds of the quarters an inexhaustible sacrificial fee in the form of fame.
He, from whose bow alone— when his enemies had laid down their weapons and its string was slackened by their prostration— there was a cessation of sound,
but not from the archers themselves;
that king’s arm was perfectly round, a friend to the sword, and dear to the heart.
He was always recognized as a hostile foe even by those who were ill-disposed toward him in battle;
having perceived that the disposition of his enemies was directed toward a single object,
he performed a particularly distinguished feat with his bow and arrows.
Other deities did not enter the cave of his heart, which was presided over by the wielder of the trident and profound with devotion; they entered it, as it were, out of fear of the fire from his eye.
He stood in the garden of the hearts of beautiful women like a thief of love.

He who, as if desiring to strike down [the senses], entered again and again without weariness; he who, though intent on yoga for the sake of tranquility, was terrifying to his enemies by his very name— for indeed,
having caught the scent of that lion among kings from afar, elephants flee in haste.

Having obtained him—who is rich in the application of the potency of mantras—as if he were her peerless bride, the Earth, who grants all desires, was fulfilled by the softness of his fingers' caress. By this much, the poetic device (*yukti*) is abandoned, even though the "jewel of beauty" (*kāntiratna*) has been displayed. (133–134ab)
He who has always extracted the entire essence of the world from the mind,
by whom the unborn Hari was made to sleep in the forest with his weapons laid aside while intent on yoga,
and by whom Rudra— who bears half the body of his beloved— was made to remember him as if desiring to conquer him.
The Fortune of his enemies wandered near the lakes of his arms like a female bee, desiring the clear wine of red honey flowing from the beds of blue lotuses;
it was endowed with a multitude of stars [or: born of a noble lineage] and provided space for all beings. 136–137ab.
He for whom even a city of water is perceived as mere empty space, like the sky;
he who, though situated in the fortress of his army and preoccupied with drawing his bow,
flees swiftly when confronted by an enemy in the forest armed only with a sword, as if standing in the midst of battle.

Even those who are hostile [to the world], absorbed in meditation, free from passion, and dwelling in caves, are not capable of attaining liberation without union with the feet of that Lord. Abandoned by my husband, who am I that I should venture to remain here among wild beasts?
Thus, as if it were a city of enemies, his own city entered the forest fire; for seeing the prowess of that courageous one in battle, the host of his foes took up residence in the forest—
which was filled with lions and other beasts— as if seeking a refuge of pure essence.
"Even one intoxicated with rut, even one who is towering, may be employed for the accomplishment of dharma"—
it was by him that the multitude of lordly elephants was bestowed in great abundance upon the twice-born.
He who established the sevenfold declension within the sphere of the primary elements (*prakṛti*).
He was devoted to the meaning of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*) and was an expert in the rules for suffixes, verbal roots, and primary nominal formations (*kṛtya*).

I suspect that the Earth, scorched by the fire of his majesty, was repeatedly drenched by him with showers of the water of his gifts, as if out of fear of being consumed by that very fire. (143cd–144)
The garland of his fame, captivating to the mind, blooming with virtues, and surpassing even the splendor of the three worlds, remains firmly held even today.
By him, the moats as deep as the ocean were reduced to ashes. (145–146)
The capital city of Campā was filled with heroes who followed the king’s commands.
His feet were pale from the luster of the jewels in the crowns of kings;
yet he held aloft a stainless earth that was devoted to all social classes.
He under whose teaching even Kali, though naturally adverse, became favorable—as if out of fear of his fiery splendor, he pursued his enemies with great speed;
and by whom the earth was rendered free of thorns from the ocean. (148–149ab)
Even today, his fame has not faltered as it has spread everywhere;

it functions primarily with respect to virtues and secondarily with respect to material things. Even the mere enumeration of him—who never abandoned the doctrine of the son of Kaśyapa—is considered a great honor.
Where indeed could he, whose every desire was for his enemies, hide himself in safety as he pleased? For when he set out, the quarters were made dark with dust;
yet she, whose mind was skilled and ever eager through love, remained fixed in her longing.
That noble lady never abandoned the royal science [of statecraft].
Dakṣa, the manifest Prajāpati, being skillful, for a moment destroys his right eye—
which is entirely flawed and a source of the defects of the Kali age.

Even in autumn, he made the sky turbid as if it were the rainy season, by means of the clouds of smoke produced from the hundreds of sacrifices he performed constantly. Though he was well-versed in virtuous conduct, he remained ever averse to the wives of others.
Someone performed the rite of taking the hands of the glories of his enemies in battle. Since the splendors of others were conquered by the rising majesty of him who was like the sun,
surely the submarine fire even today remains hidden within the ocean out of a sense of rivalry.
Surely this earth was emptied by the Lord of Serpents,
the Creator, because it has now been filled with the jewel of his own fame and marked with the bull [of Śiva].
By him, pearls were released from the temples of elephants shattered upon the field of battle.
They shed tears like drops of the illustrious widow’s weeping;
with the thundering clouds of the sound of their fame, they caused showers of wealth to fall, sowing the seeds of dharma in the field of the three worlds and making them flourish. (158cd–159)

A lion indeed is not worthy of comparison with him, whose valor in battle caused his enemy to lie hidden in a cave out of fear. Thus spoke Vāṇī, whose splendor was like that of the moon, the king of kings.
Days dawned from his countenance;
Damayantī became the royal glory of him who surpassed Kali by being united with the daughter of the King of Vidarbha.
The earth was crowded with the expansion of whose fame...
[163ab] ...with the desire to bring about the welfare of the people...
[163cd] ...him, who was of singular mind and exceeding brilliance... [164ab]
Surely the Sun was sketched by Tvaṣṭṛ after being placed upon a lathe;
for having obtained such a worthy husband in the world of mortals,
I consider Sarasvatī’s severe curse from Durvāsas to have been a blessing in disguise.
She was a savior for those desiring to cross the deep river of worldly existence—
she whose speech, though born of Satyavatī, gave birth to Vedavyāsa.
Straight by virtue of their contact with excellence, they are the warders-off of calamities.
His means of success were so vast that his arrows could not be exhausted;
surely the Creator placed this earth in the young man, lest it should shake when held by the aged Indra, who was supported by the serpent.

The sovereign power of kings, as well as the aggregate of their virtues— whether manifesting as elegance or magnanimity— seemed, as it were, to have originated from him alone. Like young maidens, the splendors of monarchs had been nurtured by him since childhood.
He who, at the proper time, employs faultless means through skillful methods;
he who has studied even the science of grammar without a teacher’s instruction on reduplication;
and he who performs his duties with diligence in all matters practiced by others—he is thus described as one who acts appropriately.
For him, no comparison whatsoever had arisen through the expansion of his virtues.
Having understood the Buddhist doctrine, he realized that it could not be otherwise even by those of other sects.
[They] were submerged in the ocean of the defects of the age, in a place difficult to traverse and profoundly terrifying.
Having reached him, as if to a lofty shore, the subjects found their rest;
he was auspicious, followed by a youth who himself followed the path of Manu,
and through him, even without elixirs, there existed an ageless state for those who had grown old.
By his brilliant splendors, scattered in every direction simultaneously,
the shadows of both the trees and the mountains were cast away.
Knowing that this was the king’s duty, he took refuge in a fortress.
The enemy of Madhu does not dwell within the ocean out of fear of the Dānavas;
rather, he has assigned even such defects as desire to their proper places and,
by his very nature, transformed them into virtues— do not speak of them otherwise.

As the world became increasingly thick with the darkness of faults, the wise drank the nectar of his poetry— which they had tasted after slaying their own minds— and along with their own verses, they vomited it forth as if from excessive drinking. (178–179)
His virtues manifested in such and such a way like lamps; he who, having by means of Dharma warded off even for the worlds the cause of destruction among those things refined by it,
did not fall into the consequence of momentary flux.
Though he had performed many sacrifices and held a high station, even the Lord of Cows (Bṛhaspati) once fell [from his position] before Indra,
who was free from anger.
In ancient times, even when encountering a fire no larger than a blade of *bhṛgu* grass, [Indra] was thwarted by him.
His splendor consumed even that great commander of armies; he, the generous one,
made his own fortune common to his friends,
[placing Lakṣmī] upon his chest.
Thirst was quenched by the beggars upon encountering him with joy—
him who was like a vast, clear lake filled with blooming lotuses,
yet one where no sun was seen, being a source of lily-like faces for women who were not his friends.
He drew [his bow] up high...
|| 185cd In that great lake of battle, where the lotus-faces of his enemies were covered by the shadows of falling arrows, the royal swan shone as he moved about. || 186ab–186cd
He who did not falter at the front of the battle was present before [his enemies],
whose reflection was cast upon his own brandishing sword.
By the mere sight of his bow, the enemies— like crows at a sacred ford— fled in haste.
Granted that even the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) could not stand before him in battle;
he who [offered] a path to his fleeing enemies— those warriors whose arrows were like blossoming flowers amidst the lovely groves of *sāla* trees.
By him, the city of Virāṭa was made empty of enemies— though once filled with hundreds of towering Kīcakas and inhabited by Kaṅka and others—
while he extracted only the heroic power of the kings, like a spell draws out the essence of medicinal herbs.
He who, like Tārkṣya upon the earth, did not waste his vital breaths through gluttony—
seeing whose sacrifice,
Śacī surely shed tears from her eyes under the pretext of contact with smoke, fearing the ruin of Indra’s glory.
The lords of the quarters, who had obstructed the splendor of others, constantly sought refuge in the shadow of his feet,
just as the guardians of the oceans resort to Mount Meru;
he was like the Creator, who, out of disregard, created the sun and moon as if they were separate from one another.
He alone he rendered peerless, capable of both scorching and gladdening.
Desiring to serve at his side, the rows of kings sprinkled his feet— possessing such intense brilliance— with the waters of the luster from the jewels in their crowns.
Ah, what a new and wonderful thing in this world: that Smara, having cast aside his bow,
has agitated the hearts of women by means of his incomparable splendor—
[a splendor] which is like a lotus with the eight quarters as its clearly visible petals and the golden mountain as its great pericarp.
The fame of him who [shines] upon the unique lotus of the world spreads like a fragrance;
the rays from the nails of his feet, vibrating with an outpoured redness,
vied with the luster of the crest-jewels of bowing kings.

Just as Dilīpa, even a mango tree that had been barren since its birth, came under his command for the sake of the abundant production of fruit; so too did [the world] come under the command of Vasiṣṭha,
whose profound expansion of virtues was celebrated by a thousand mouths.
Having obtained his commentary, even the intellects of the wise were exhausted [in attempting to explain it].
On the mountain Śivapura, he established the illustrious Siddheśvara Liṅga and honored it with unprecedented enjoyments such as palanquins and other offerings.
There too, he properly installed the auspicious image of Śarvāṇī, together with the Liṅga of Śarva,
for the increase of the merit of his ancestors;
beginning from that very point, the presence of the Blessed Lord Bhadreśvara, the Wielder of the Trident, was established.
That moon among kings, Śrī Indravarman and his successors, increased the prosperity of the oceans of dharma elsewhere as well through their worship of the gods,
and he likewise brought about the simultaneous expansion of his own realm.
To the south of the Yaśodhara tank is also the southern [shrine] (205ab),
where Śauri, Gaurīśa, and Śani [are located]. That King Rājendravarma, the sun in the sky of the Lunar dynasty, established this liṅga of Śambhu (205cd–206ab).

The lord of the earth, whose fame had been attained, established a linga of the Enemy of Smara as a sign for the attainment of heaven and liberation; and he, who knew the principles of stability, likewise established these two Nimes— the abodes of Śiva and Śivā— in proximity to one another for the welfare of the world, following the example set by his parents who had reached that state through the grace of the Lord of Beings.

Having completed his royal duties, that mighty-armed king also consecrated this image of the four-armed one born from the lotus, as well as the eight lingas of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva). He also established an inexhaustible heap of wealth, radiant with thousands of coils shimmering with jewels.
Like Aditi among the gods,
he who possessed prowess equal to the Lord of the Gods established for all these [deities] a complete and perpetual code of righteous conduct,
as well as a sufficient ritual worship for these deities here, as prescribed by the Śaiva scriptures and the Smṛtis.

And he, whose intellect was like that of Vācaspati, steadfast, a follower of dharma, and the leader of those who uphold the law, spoke these words to the lords of Kambuja regarding those future kings who were to cultivate the duties of sovereignty:
"The protection of that which is to be protected... for when that duty of the kṣatriya is ordained for you by fate..."
The request, "Protect this very merit," as if accomplishing what was already achieved, [seems to say]:

"In this age, Dharma stands on only one foot; how would it have remained well-established if it had not relied upon the pillar-like arm of a person like you, who possesses the vision of the scriptures? Who indeed, being virtuous, would feel shame to be the author of a calamity for Dharma—how much more so if it were done by oneself?
It is well known to you that the king is especially the guardian of this [earth].

(214cd) The virtuous, whose wealth is fame and dharma, do not desire external wealth even for themselves in this world; how much less so the wealth of gods and others? This resolve of yours, O virtuous ones, is indeed firmly rooted. (215ab–215cd)
Nevertheless, I speak to you once more: protect this merit of yours unimpaired. To say "do not take the property of the gods" aloud is not a fault of redundancy for the sake of dharma.
When entreated, a great man would give even his own life through the power of his magnanimity; how much more so his own possessions?
And therefore, this request in speech— bold through the power of confidence and free from the fear of rejection—

is made on the meritorious eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when the Śaka year is reckoned by the [number] of the elephants (8) and the Vasus (8), while the moon has entered its sixth year. (217cd–218ab)

Together with these images of Śauri, Gaurī, Giriśa, and the Daughter of the Mountain, this [image] of the crescent-crested Lord established that supreme liṅga here known as Śrī Rājendreśvara. || 218cd ||
